questions.questionText: SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks). Choose EITHER Question 1(a) OR Question 1(b). Spend about 1 hour on this section. Write your answer in 80-120 words. Either (a): You have been asked to speak at your school assembly to encourage younger pupils to take care of the environment. Write the speech you will give. Use the following points and any others you may think of: why the environment must be protected; one problem caused by littering or cutting down trees; what pupils can do to help; who can support them (teachers, parents, community leaders); and why this matters for the future.
questions.explanation:
**Speech Plan & Model Guide [20 marks]:** Address the assembly politely: *"The School Head, respected teachers, and dear younger learners, good morning."* **Paragraph 1 (Why Environment Matters & One Problem):** Hook peers immediately on how our trees, clean grounds, and nearby streams give us fresh air, shade, and safe play—before warning clearly against **littering and careless tree-cutting**, explaining how dropped plastic chokes drains/livestock while felling saplings turns fields dusty and eroded.

**Paragraph 2 (Actions Pupils Can Take & Community Support):** Lay out **three fun, practical youth habits**—using litter bins consistently, watering and protecting newly planted school trees, and sorting bottles/paper cleanly—reminding younger pupils that **teachers, parents, and village/community leaders** stand ready to supply tools, fenced beds, and encouragement whenever classes lead weekly clean-ups.

**Paragraph 3 (Why It Matters for the Future):** Conclude powerfully explaining that protecting trees and soil today preserves shade, fruit, clean water, and fertile farmland for younger brothers and sisters long into tomorrow, ending warmly with **"Let us guard our green school together—thank you!"** Keep strictly around 100–130 words and never use letter addresses.

questions.questionText: SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks). Choose EITHER Question 1(a) OR Question 1(b). Spend about 1 hour on this section. Write your answer in 80-120 words. Or (b): Write a composition describing a memorable day you spent helping at a family or community event (for example a wedding, a harvest, or a family gathering). Use the following points and any others you may think of: what the event was; where and when it took place; who else was there; what your role or job was on the day; and why you will always remember it.
questions.explanation:
**Descriptive Composition Guide — Helping at a Family or Community Event [20 marks]:** **Paragraph 1 (Event, Place, Time & People):** Establish a joyful realistic gathering smoothly—such as a cousin’s traditional wedding in Murewa or a village cooperative maize harvest/church celebration on a crisp bright Saturday morning—naming relatives, neighbours, drummers, and cheerful aunts bustling around outdoor cooking fires.

**Paragraph 2 (Your Specific Role):** Describe clearly and proudly what responsible job you performed on the day—for instance, leading younger cousins in carrying clean water buckets to handwashing stations, arranging wooden chairs neatly under white canvas tents, serving warm plates politely to visiting elders using both hands in true ***Unhu/Ubuntu*** courtesy, and helping clear cups without dropping one tray.

**Paragraph 3 (Reflection & Lasting Memory):** Close meaningfully explaining why that joyful teamwork, music, and warm praise from grandparents (*"Our young host truly saved the morning!"*) made you feel proud, grown-up, and connected closely to family hospitality forever.

SECTION B - COMPREHENSION (15 marks). Spend about 45 minutes on this section. Read the passage carefully, then answer the questions that follow in full, grammatically correct sentences.

VICTORIA FALLS: THE SMOKE THAT THUNDERS

Victoria Falls is one of Zimbabwe's greatest natural treasures. Local people have long called it "Mosi-oa-Tunya," which means "the smoke that thunders," because the huge cloud of spray rising from the falls can be seen from many kilometres away, and the roar of the crashing water sounds like distant thunder.

The falls were formed over millions of years as the mighty Zambezi River wore away layers of soft rock, leaving behind a deep, narrow gorge with hard basalt walls on either side. Today, the river plunges more than one hundred metres into this gorge, creating one of the largest curtains of falling water found anywhere on Earth.

Every year, thousands of visitors from Zimbabwe and from other countries travel to see the falls. Tourism built around Victoria Falls provides jobs for many local people, who work as tour guides, hotel staff, curio sellers and boat operators. This income helps to support families and to fund the conservation of the surrounding national park.

However, the falls and the wildlife around them face growing threats. Pollution of the Zambezi River, the cutting down of nearby trees, and the effects of changing rainfall patterns all put pressure on this fragile environment. Conservationists warn that without careful management, both the beauty of the falls and the livelihoods that depend on them could be damaged.

Despite these challenges, Victoria Falls remains a proud symbol of Zimbabwe's natural heritage, drawing visitors and admiration from all over the world.

Question (a): Give a metaphor used in paragraph 1 to describe the sound of the falls.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [1–2 marks]:** The metaphor in Paragraph 1 used to describe the powerful sound of Victoria Falls is **"the smoke that thunders"** (*or specifically calling the roar of falling water **"thunder"** / comparing its sound directly to **"the roar of distant thunder"** via indigenous Lozi/Tonga name **"Mosi-oa-Tunya"***) [2 marks].

Notice how **"the smoke that thunders"** works figuratively without literal fire or lightning: the huge rising mist cloud looks vividly like wood-smoke drifting skyward while the booming crash of plunging Zambezi water shakes the basalt gorge like a storm. Look carefully at the distinction between **metaphor** (identifying one thing *as* another directly: *"Mosi-oa-Tunya — the smoke that thunders"*) and **simile** (explicitly using *"like"* or *"as"* in *"sounds like distant thunder"*).

In ZIMSEC Comprehension Paper 2, state the **exact quoted phrase from Paragraph 1** inside quotation marks (**"the smoke that thunders"**) in a full sentence explaining both its sound imagery and local name.

Question (b): What shows that Victoria Falls is important to Zimbabwe's economy?
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Three specific pieces of passage evidence show Victoria Falls’ vital importance to **Zimbabwe’s economy**: **(1) Tourism attracts thousands of domestic and international visitors annually**, **(2) Tourism creates steady jobs for local guides, hotel workers, curio/craft sellers, and boat operators supporting entire families**, and **(3) Tourism revenue helps fund conservation of the surrounding national park** [2 marks].

When marking Paragraph 3, ZIMSEC examiners separate *scenic beauty* (*"biggest waterfall"*) from *economic benefit* (*"jobs, family income, and national park funding"*). Reading closely ensures you pick employment and park-funding facts rather than geological gorge history from Paragraph 2.

Write your answer in your own clean complete sentence referencing **thousands of tourists, local jobs (guides, hotel staff, curio sellers, boat operators), family income, and park conservation funds** cleanly.

Question (c): How were the falls formed?
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** According to Paragraph 2, Victoria Falls formed **over millions of years as the powerful Zambezi River gradually wore away (eroded) bands of soft rock, leaving behind a deep, narrow gorge flanked by hard basalt rock walls** down which the water plunges more than one hundred metres [2 marks].

Geologically, river water rushing over alternating hard basalt and softer faulted rock cracks along the Zambezi riverbed etched out a zigzag series of deep narrow gorges over millennia—turning gentle wide river currents into one massive perpendicular curtain of plunging water over 100 m deep.

Avoid copying Paragraph 2 blindly word-for-word; summarise the process clearly with key science/comprehension ideas (**erosion of soft rock by the Zambezi River over millions of years, leaving hard basalt gorge walls**).

Question (k) SUMMARY (5 marks): In not more than 50 words, summarise the benefits AND the threats to Victoria Falls described in the passage. Begin your summary as follows: 'Victoria Falls benefits Zimbabwe by....'
questions.explanation:
**Model 50-Word Summary [5 marks]:** *Victoria Falls benefits Zimbabwe by attracting thousands of visitors yearly, providing vital jobs and family income for local guides, hotel workers, curio sellers, and boat operators, and funding park conservation; however, it faces growing threats from Zambezi River pollution, local deforestation, and shifting rainfall patterns.* (46 words.)

Look carefully at the two compulsory halves in Question (k): **"summarise the benefits AND the threats to Victoria Falls"** starting verbatim with **"Victoria Falls benefits Zimbabwe by..."**. In **46 tight words**, the first half covers **benefits** (tourism/visitors, local jobs/income across guides/hotels/curio/boats, park conservation funding) before **"; however, it faces threats from..."** pivots smoothly into all three **threats** (river pollution, cutting trees/deforestation, changing rainfall)!

Counting every word carefully keeps total length safely below the **50-word limit** while securing maximum Content (4/4) and Grammar (+1) marks.

questions.questionText:
**Passage:**
The school library had been neglected for several years. Books were dusty, some shelves were broken and many learners preferred to spend their free time outside. A new librarian decided to change the situation. She organised the books, repaired the shelves with the help of the school maintenance team and started a reading club. Within a few months, learners were borrowing books regularly and discussing stories during break time.

Read the passage carefully. Answer the questions that follow. Passage 1.
- (a) Give one reason why the learners initially avoided the library. [1 mark]
- (b) State two actions taken by the new librarian. [2 marks]
- (c) What evidence shows that the changes were successful? [2 marks]
- (d) Give a suitable title for the passage. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Comprehension Answers [6 marks]:** **(a)** Learners initially avoided the library because the books were covered in dust and several bookshelves were broken [1 mark]. **(b)** The new librarian took three decisive actions (any two required): she sorted and organised the books neatly, worked with the school maintenance team to repair broken shelves, and launched a reading club [2 marks]. **(c)** Two pieces of evidence prove the revival succeeded: within a few months learners began borrowing books regularly and discussing stories enthusiastically during break time [2 marks]. **(d)** A suitable concise title reflecting the central idea is **"Reviving the School Library"** or **"The New Librarian’s Transformation"** [1 mark].

Notice how every answer above demonstrates proper **ZIMSEC 7010/2 full-sentence comprehension technique**: rather than writing fragmented phrases such as "dusty books", restating the question stem (*"Learners initially avoided the library because..."*) keeps subject-verb agreement intact and earns guaranteed marks. In part (b), counting the exact command number (**"two actions"**) stops you from wasting precious minutes copying a third extra point when the mark scheme caps part (b) at 2 marks.

A common national error in Paper 2 passage comprehension is wholesale copying ("lifting") of long lines containing irrelevant facts. Always read every clue carefully, select only the exact evidence answering *why*, *what actions*, or *what proof*, and keep titles short (3–6 words without ending punctuation).

questions.questionText:
Rewrite the sentence in the plural: 'The child carried a box to the classroom.'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence correctly in the plural. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Grammar Answer [2 marks]:** Converted correctly into plural form, the sentence becomes: **"The children carried boxes to the classrooms."** [2 marks]. Notice every countable noun changes simultaneously while the past-tense verb remains unchanged: **child → children** (irregular plural—never write "childs"), **a box → boxes** (adding **-es** after **-x** and dropping the singular indefinite article **a**), and **classroom → classrooms** (regular **-s** plural).

In English grammar, converting a sentence from singular to plural demands checking three things systematically from left to right: **(1) determiners/articles** (*a* or *an* cannot appear before plural countable nouns, so drop *a* or change to *some/the*), **(2) irregular and regular noun endings** (*child → children*, *box → boxes* following the *-s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z → -es* rule), and **(3) verb tense agreement** (since **carried** is simple past tense, it stays identical for both singular *"the child carried"* and plural *"the children carried"*).

Grade 7 markers regularly penalise two classic mistakes: writing *"childrens"* or *"the children carried a boxes"* (forgetting to delete **a** before the plural **boxes**), or leaving **"the classroom"** singular while pluralising the rest. Check every noun one by one before writing your final sentence.

questions.questionText:
Correct the error in the sentence: 'Neither of the boys have completed the task.'
- (a) Write the corrected sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Grammar Correction [2 marks]:** The grammatically corrected sentence is: **"Neither of the boys has completed the task."** [2 marks]. The error lies in the plural verb **"have"**, which must be replaced with the singular auxiliary verb **"has"** because the distributive pronoun **"Neither"** refers to *not one individual boy* out of the pair and always governs a singular verb.

Many learners get tricked by the plural noun **"boys"** standing right beside the verb inside the prepositional phrase *"of the boys"*. Remember the ZIMSEC subject-verb concord rule: words such as **each, either, neither, everyone, somebody, and nobody** act strictly as singular subjects regardless of any plural nouns inside *"of the ..."* (for instance: *"Neither of the girls **is** absent"*, *"Each of the learners **was** given a ruler"*).

When answering error-correction items in Paper 2, write out the **complete corrected sentence** neatly rather than circling or writing just the single word *"has"* unless specifically told otherwise—and read aloud mentally with *"Neither one..."* to verify smooth singular agreement.

questions.questionText:
Join the sentences using 'although': 'The road was muddy. The bus continued its journey.'
- (a) Write one correct combined sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Conjunction Answer [2 marks]:** Combined smoothly using the subordinating conjunction **"although"**, the correct sentence is: **"Although the road was muddy, the bus continued its journey."** (Equally valid: **"The bus continued its journey although the road was muddy."**) [2 marks].

**Although** expresses **concession / contrast** between two clauses where the second outcome happens unexpectedly despite an obstacle in the first clause—unlike *because* (cause) or *and* (addition). Grammar punctuation matters too: when the subordinate *Although...* clause comes **first**, place a **comma** cleanly after *"muddy,"* before starting the main clause (*"the bus continued its journey"*); when *although* sits in the middle between clauses, no comma is usually needed.

The commonest ZIMSEC error when combining sentences with *although* is leaving **"but"** inside the same sentence (*"Although the road was muddy, but the bus continued"*—wrong! Never pair *although* with *but*!). Use **either** *although* **or** *but*, never both together.

questions.questionText:
Rewrite the sentence in the past tense: 'The learners clean the classroom every Friday.'
- (a) Write the sentence in the past tense. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Tense Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten accurately in the **simple past tense**, the sentence reads: **"The learners cleaned the classroom every Friday."** (Or referring to a specific past occasion: *"The learners cleaned the classroom last Friday."*) [2 marks]. The regular present-tense verb **"clean"** adds **-ed** to form the simple past **"cleaned"** while keeping the rest of the sentence intact.

Changing tenses in ZIMSEC language sections focuses sharply on identifying the **finite verb** carrying time: in *"The learners clean..."*, plural subject *learners* pairs with base form *clean* indicating a present habit. Switching to simple past requires **-ed** on regular verbs (*clean → cleaned*)—never adding unnecessary helping words like *"were cleaned"* (passive!) or *"did cleaned"* (double past!).

Always verify spelling and voice: writing *"The learners were clean"* changes the meaning into an adjective instead of a past action, whereas **The learners cleaned the classroom every Friday** preserves active subject-action meaning cleanly.

questions.questionText:
Replace the underlined noun phrase with a suitable pronoun: 'Rudo and Chipo carried the books.'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence using an appropriate pronoun. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Pronoun Answer [2 marks]:** Replacing the compound plural noun phrase **"Rudo and Chipo"** with the matching subject pronoun yields: **"They carried the books."** [2 marks]. Because Rudo and Chipo together form a **third-person plural subject** performing the action (*carried*), the correct nominative plural pronoun is **"They"** (never *"Them"* or *"She"*).

Pronoun substitution in Grade 7 grammar requires testing both **number** (one person vs two or more people) and **grammatical case** (**subject** vs **object**). When replacing the doer before the verb (*"Rudo and Chipo carried..."*), choose subject pronoun **They**; had their names appeared *after* a verb or preposition (*"The teacher praised Rudo and Chipo"*), you would choose object pronoun **them** (*"The teacher praised them"*).

Learners occasionally write ungrammatical dialect forms like *"Them carried the books"* or *"They two carried"*. Always capitalise **They** at the start of the sentence and read it back carefully to confirm crisp standard English.

questions.questionText:
Rewrite using 'not only...but also': 'The club teaches reading. The club teaches writing.'
- (a) Write the combined sentence. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Correlative Conjunction Answer [2 marks]:** Joined cleanly using **"not only ... but also"**, the sentence becomes: **"The club teaches not only reading but also writing."** [2 marks]. Notice that parallel grammatical items—two gerund nouns (**reading** and **writing**)—follow immediately after *"not only"* and *"but also"* without repeating *"The club teaches"* twice unnecessarily.

The correlative pair **not only … but also …** emphasises that two balanced facts are both true. To maintain **parallel structure**, place *"not only"* right before the first differing element (*reading*) rather than too early (*"Not only the club teaches reading"* shifts subject position awkwardly): keep the shared opening **"The club teaches"** once, then link **not only [Item 1] but also [Item 2]**.

ZIMSEC markers deduct marks if candidates misspell **"also"** or write *"not only reading, but writing too"* missing the required **"but also"** phrase, or leave both sentences loosely fused with a comma. Double-check exact parallel balance around **"not only"** and **"but also"**.

questions.questionText:
Change the direct speech into reported speech: 'I am ready,' Tendai said.
- (a) Write the sentence in reported speech. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Reported Speech Answer [2 marks]:** Changed accurately from direct speech into **reported (indirect) speech**, the sentence becomes: **"Tendai said that he was ready."** (Or **"Tendai said that she was ready."**) [2 marks]. Notice all four required adjustments: remove quotation marks and comma, add optional reporting conjunction **"that"**, shift pronoun **"I" → "he/she"**, and backshift present tense **"am" → past tense "was"**.

Reported speech shifts a speaker’s exact spoken words (**"I am ready"**) back in time from the narrator’s perspective after a past reporting verb (**said**). Because the speaker is Tendai, first-person *"I"* becomes third-person **he** or **she**, and present linking verb *"am"* steps back one tense into **was**—while retaining the speaker’s exact meaning cleanly without speech marks.

The top Grade 7 errors in reported speech are forgetting to remove quotation marks ('Tendai said that "he was ready"'—wrong!) or failing to backshift the verb ('Tendai said that he is ready'). Always verify **zero speech marks**, **pronoun match**, and **past-tense backshift ('am → was')**.

questions.questionText:
Add the missing punctuation: 'what a beautiful garden said the visitor'
- (a) Rewrite the sentence with correct punctuation. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Punctuation Answer [2 marks]:** Rewritten with accurate capitalisation, quotation marks, and end-of-quote exclamation/punctuation, the sentence reads: **"What a beautiful garden!" said the visitor.** (Also acceptable: *"What a beautiful garden," said the visitor.*) [2 marks]. Notice **W** is capitalised at the start of direct speech, opening/closing inverted commas **'"..."'** wrap ONLY the spoken words, an exclamation mark **'!'** (or comma) sits *inside* the closing quotation mark before *"said"*, and a full stop ends the reporting clause after **visitor.**

Punctuating direct speech cleanly separates **what was actually spoken aloud** from **who spoke it**. Because *"What a beautiful garden!"* expresses strong admiration beginning with exclamatory *"What a..."*, an exclamation mark inside the closing inverted commas ('!"') captures tone far better than a bare comma, yet *"said"* still begins with a lowercase **s** because *"said the visitor"* finishes the same single grammatical sentence!

Candidates routinely lose punctuation marks in Paper 2 by forgetting either opening/closing speech marks, missing the closing **full stop after 'visitor.'**, or mistakenly capitalising 'Said' after an exclamation mark inside dialogue. Inspect every boundary carefully.

questions.questionText:
Give an antonym for the underlined word: 'The water was shallow.'
- (a) Write the opposite of 'shallow'. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Vocabulary Answer [1–2 marks]:** The direct antonym (word opposite in meaning) for **"shallow"** in *"The water was shallow"* is **"deep"** [1 mark]. Rewritten cleanly in context: **"The water was deep."**

An **antonym** contrasts opposite qualities along the same scale of meaning while keeping the **exact same part of speech**. Here *"shallow"* functions as a descriptive **adjective** describing low vertical depth of water; therefore its precise adjective opposite is **deep** (avoid loose phrases like *"not shallow"* or unrelated words like *"high"* or *"wide"*, which measure horizontal breadth or elevation rather than downward water depth!).

In ZIMSEC English Paper 2, check whether the instruction asks for a **single word opposite** (**deep**) or to **rewrite the whole sentence with the opposite**. Giving both the exact word (**deep**) and its contextual sentence guarantees zero lost marks.

questions.questionText:
Give a synonym for the underlined word: 'The villagers were delighted.'
- (a) Write one word with a similar meaning to 'delighted'. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Vocabulary Answer [1–2 marks]:** Accurate single-word **synonyms** (words closest in meaning) for **"delighted"** in *"The villagers were delighted"* are **"overjoyed"**, **"thrilled"**, **"pleased"**, **"glad"**, or **"happy"** [1 mark]. In context: **"The villagers were overjoyed."**

Choosing an accurate synonym means matching both **meaning intensity** and **grammatical word class**. Since *"delighted"* is a past-participle/adjective expressing warm great happiness, **overjoyed** or **thrilled** mirrors its strong positive intensity best, whereas **pleased** and **happy** also fit smoothly in standard Grade 7 grammar without changing tense or plural agreement (*"were overjoyed"*).

Never supply an explanatory phrase (like *"feeling good"*) when the exam specifically requests **one word** with a similar meaning—stick strictly to one crisp adjective (**overjoyed / thrilled / pleased**) that slots directly into *"The villagers were ____."*

questions.questionText:
Write a friendly letter to a cousin describing a memorable school event.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Friendly Letter Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Follow official **ZIMSEC 7010/2 Informal (Friendly) Letter Format**: **(1) Top right:** Write ONE address only—your own street/school address with date below (e.g., *Mupfure Primary School, P.O. Box 42, Chegutu, 18 October 2026*) [3 marks]; **(2) Left margin:** Warm salutation (*"Dear Cousin Tatenda,"*) [1 mark]; **(3) Opening paragraph:** Friendly greeting asking about aunt, uncle, and cousin’s schoolwork before introducing your memorable event (for instance, Inter-House Athletics Day or Grade 7 Heritage Cultural Festival) [4 marks]; **(4) Body paragraphs (2–3 paragraphs):** Describe **when and where** it happened, **vivid sights and sounds** (drumming, cheering, winning the 4×100 m relay or cultural dance), and **how you felt** using expressive verbs and sensory adjectives [11 marks]; **(5) Warm closing & sign-off:** Brief farewell sending greetings home plus *"Your loving cousin, Chipo"* (first name only) [6 marks for layout close + grammar].

Keeping **consistent past tense** throughout your narrative (*cheered, sprinted, beamed, celebrated*) alongside lively dialogue or personal reflection makes a friendly letter sound natural, warm, and genuinely engaging rather than reading like a stiff list of times. Vary your sentence openings (*"As soon as the whistle blew...", "To my surprise..."*) and write comfortably around 120–150 focused words across 4 clear paragraphs.

Two big ZIMSEC Paper 2 traps sink otherwise strong friendly letters: accidentally writing **two addresses** (only *formal* letters use recipient addresses!), and signing off stiffly with *"Yours faithfully, Chipo Moyo"* instead of warm informal sign-offs (**"Your loving cousin,"** or **"Yours affectionately,"** + first name).

questions.questionText:
Write a formal letter to the head of your school suggesting two ways of improving the school grounds.
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Formal Letter Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Follow strict **ZIMSEC 7010/2 Formal Business Letter Format**: **(1) Top right / block format:** Your own sender’s address + date; **(2) Left margin:** Recipient’s official title & school address (*The Head, [School Name], P.O. Box ...*) [4 marks]; **(3) Salutation & Heading:** *"Dear Sir/Madam,"* followed by a **concise underlined/bold subject line** (*RE: SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVING THE SCHOOL GROUNDS*) [3 marks]; **(4) Focused Body Paragraphs:** Paragraph 1 states politely why you are writing as a concerned Grade 7 prefect/learner. Paragraph 2 explains **Suggestion 1** clearly (e.g., planting indigenous shade trees and flowerbeds around walkways with duty rosters so erosion and dust drop). Paragraph 3 explains **Suggestion 2** (e.g., placing labelled colour-coded litter bins and paved stone footpaths to stop mud being tracked into classrooms) [12 marks]; **(5) Polite close & full sign-off:** Hope-for-action closing followed by **"Yours faithfully,"** (when using *Sir/Madam*), handwritten signature, and your **full name** (**Tendai Moyo**) [6 marks].

Register in a formal letter must stay polite, respectful, persuasive, and free of slang or contractions (*write "cannot" and "it would improve" instead of "can't" or "wanna"*). Backing up each practical suggestion with clear benefits—cooler shade during breaks, cleaner classrooms, and proud visitors—persuades examiners you understand real problem-solving.

Markers frequently deduct layout marks when candidates omit the **recipient’s address**, forget **RE: SUBJECT HEADING**, write informal greetings (*"How are you, Headmaster?"*), or mix **"Dear Sir/Madam"** with **"Yours sincerely"** (remember: *Dear Sir/Madam → **Yours faithfully**; Dear Mr Moyo → **Yours sincerely***).

questions.questionText:
Write a story beginning with: 'When I opened the old wooden box, I could not believe what I saw.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Narrative Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Begin **word-for-word** with the required opening sentence without altering a single punctuation mark: **"When I opened the old wooden box, I could not believe what I saw."** [2 marks]. **Paragraph 1 (Hook & Discovery):** Establish *where* you found the dusty box (e.g., cleaning Grandmother’s old storeroom during August holidays) and **reveal an intriguing, believable object inside**—such as a faded hand-carved soapstone bird wrapper, yellowed 1980 Independence newspaper clippings, or a brass pocket watch and family photographs [5 marks]. **Paragraphs 2–3 (Rising Mystery & Explanation):** Describe your amazement using vivid sensory clues (*creaking hinges, smell of cedarwood, trembling fingers*) and share how an elder/Grandmother entered and revealed the inspiring backstory connecting your family to perseverance or heritage [10 marks]. **Paragraph 4 (Reflection & Resolution):** End meaningfully explaining how guarding that heirloom taught gratitude and pride in family roots [8 marks for style & accuracy].

Strong Grade 7 stories stay **credible and tightly focused** around one brief afternoon scene rather than wandering into wild impossible adventures (avoid ending abruptly with *"and then I woke up from a dream"*—ZIMSEC markers penalise cliché dream endings!). Using strong descriptive verbs (*creaked, gleamed, whispered*) and one or two short lines of punctuated dialogue lifts Language marks dramatically.

Always double-check that you copied the prompt’s exact opening sentence smoothly into Paragraph 1 and checked past-tense verbs, commas, and quotation marks across every paragraph.

questions.questionText:
Write a composition on: 'The importance of keeping our community clean.'
- (a) Write your response in continuous prose, observing appropriate structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Expository Composition Plan & Model Guide [25 marks]:** Structure **"The importance of keeping our community clean"** across 4 cohesive paragraphs: **(1) Introduction:** Define a clean community environment (litter-free streets, unblocked drains, clean water points, trimmed verges) and state clearly that environmental cleanliness protects public health, safety, and civic pride [4 marks]. **(2) Body Paragraph 1 — Health & Disease Prevention:** Explain concretely how clearing rotting waste and stagnant puddles destroys breeding places for **houseflies, rats, and malaria mosquitoes**, dramatically cutting cholera, typhoid, and diarrhoea outbreaks among young children [6 marks]. **(3) Body Paragraph 2 — Safety, Environment & Pride:** Detail how proper bins and avoiding burning plastic keep air breathable, prevent plastic litter from choking livestock or storm drains, protect streams from runoff pollution, and make markets and schools welcoming for visitors [6 marks]. **(4) Conclusion — Practical Actions:** Call on households, youth clubs, and councils to practise *Reduce–Reuse–Recycle*, compost organic scraps, and join monthly national clean-up days [9 marks for structure & language accuracy].

Expository essays earn top ZIMSEC marks through **clear logical topic sentences** (*"First and most urgently, a clean neighbourhood safeguards every family’s health..."*) paired with real Zimbabwean illustrations rather than repetitive empty slogans (*"Cleanliness is good, keep clean"*).

Check spelling of tricky environmental words (**environment, hygiene, mosquitoes, diarrhoea, community, responsibility**) and avoid informal second-person lecturing (*"You must stop littering!"*)—prefer inclusive civic voice (*"Every resident and learner shares a duty to..."*).
